body:
What is momentum?

Momentum describes the motion of an object by combining its mass and velocity. An object with a larger mass or greater speed has greater momentum in magnitude when the other quantity remains unchanged.

For an object of mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(v\), momentum \(p\) is:

$$p=mv$$

Momentum is a vector quantity. Its direction is the same as the direction of velocity. Its SI unit is kg m/s.

For example, a 2 kg object moving east at 3 m/s has momentum 6 kg m/s east. A stationary object has zero momentum, even if its mass is large.

Newton's second law of motion

Newton's second law relates the net external force acting on an object to the rate of change of its momentum. The change in momentum occurs in the direction of the net force.

For a constant net force acting over a time interval:

$$F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$

For a body of constant mass, this becomes:

$$F=ma$$

Here, \(F\) is the net force, \(m\) is mass and \(a\) is acceleration.

1 newton is the net force required to produce an acceleration of 1 m/s2 in an object of mass 1 kg.

$$1\ \text{N}=1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$$

How mass and force affect acceleration

For a fixed mass, doubling the net force doubles the acceleration. For a fixed net force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.

Suppose the same net force of 6 N acts separately on a 2 kg object and a 3 kg object. Their accelerations are:

$$a_1=\frac{6}{2}=3\ \text{m/s}^2$$

$$a_2=\frac{6}{3}=2\ \text{m/s}^2$$

Worked example: Finding force from a change in velocity

A 2 kg object moving along a straight line changes velocity uniformly from 3 m/s to 7 m/s in 2 s.

Acceleration:

$$a=\frac{7-3}{2}=2\ \text{m/s}^2$$

Net force:

$$F=2\times2=4\ \text{N}$$

Initial momentum is \(2\times3=6\) kg m/s and final momentum is \(2\times7=14\) kg m/s. The change in momentum is therefore 8 kg m/s.

Dividing this momentum change by 2 s again gives the net force, \(8/2=4\) N.

Why increasing stopping time reduces impact force

When a cricket fielder catches a moving ball, the ball's momentum must decrease to zero relative to the ground. If the fielder brings the hands backwards with the ball, the stopping time increases.

For the same change in momentum, a longer stopping time means a smaller average force on the ball and the hands. A padded surface similarly increases the stopping time during an impact.

The relationship is expressed as:

$$F_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$

Thus, reducing the rate of change of momentum reduces the magnitude of the average force required for the same momentum change.

Prelims focus

  • Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity.
  • Momentum is a vector with SI unit kg m/s.
  • Newton's second law connects net force with the rate of change of momentum.
  • For constant mass, net force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.
  • 1 N produces 1 m/s2 acceleration in a 1 kg mass.
  • Trap: Greater mass does not imply greater acceleration under the same net force.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, 'Force and Laws of Motion', section 9.4, pp. 119–122, 2018–19 print; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 'Force and Laws of Motion', section on the second law of motion, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Newton's Second Law: Momentum, Force and Acceleration

body:
Every force arises through an interaction

Newton's third law of motion states that when one object exerts a force on another object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal force in the opposite direction on the first object.

These forces form an action–reaction pair. They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, but they act on different objects.

Action and reaction forces do not cancel each other when calculating the net force on one object because each force acts on a different object.

Example: Walking on the ground

While walking forward, a person's foot pushes the ground backwards. The ground exerts a forward frictional force on the foot. This forward force helps the person accelerate.

The backward force on the ground and the forward force on the foot form a third-law pair. Both forces occur simultaneously.

When a person pushes a wall, the wall pushes back with an equal and opposite force. The wall may remain stationary because its motion depends on the complete set of forces acting on it, not merely on the force exerted by the person.

Balanced forces versus action–reaction forces

FeatureBalanced forcesAction–reaction pair
Act onThe same objectDifferent objects
Result on one objectNet force is zeroDo not cancel on one object
ConditionForces sum to zeroEqual and opposite by the third law

What is conservation of momentum?

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity. For an isolated system, where the net external force is zero, the total momentum remains constant.

During a collision, interacting objects exert equal and opposite forces on one another. These internal forces may change each object's momentum, but they do not change the total momentum of the isolated system.

This principle is called the law of conservation of momentum.

For 2 objects moving along the same straight line:

$$m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2$$

Here, \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are their masses; \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) are velocities before interaction; and \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) are velocities after interaction. Velocities must be assigned positive or negative signs according to their directions.

Worked example: Two trolleys stick together

A 2 kg trolley moves to the right at 3 m/s and collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Assume the net external horizontal force during the collision is negligible.

Choose right as positive. Initial momentum:

$$p_i=(2\times3)+(1\times0)=6\ \text{kg m/s}$$

After the collision, the combined mass is 3 kg. If the common velocity is \(v\), conservation of momentum gives:

$$3v=6\quad\Rightarrow\quad v=2\ \text{m/s}$$

Both trolleys therefore move to the right at 2 m/s immediately after the collision.

Before collision, the first trolley has momentum 6 kg m/s and the second has zero. After collision, their momenta are 4 kg m/s and 2 kg m/s respectively. Their sum is still 6 kg m/s.

Important conditions and distinctions

Momentum conservation concerns the total momentum of the system, not necessarily the momentum of each individual object. It applies when the net external force is zero, or is negligible during the short interaction being considered.

If objects move in opposite directions, their momenta must be added with opposite signs. Momentum is a vector, so direction matters.

In a collision where objects stick together, total momentum can be conserved even though kinetic energy is not conserved as kinetic energy.

Prelims focus

  • Action and reaction forces are simultaneous, equal and opposite.
  • They act on different objects.
  • Third-law force pairs do not cancel on a single object.
  • Total momentum is conserved when the net external force on the system is zero.
  • Opposite-direction momenta must be combined using signs.
  • Trap: Conservation of total momentum does not mean each object's momentum remains unchanged.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, 'Force and Laws of Motion', sections 9.5 and 9.6, pp. 122–127, 2018–19 print.]

title: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Momentum

body:
What is friction?

Friction is a contact force that opposes relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between surfaces in contact.

When a book slides across a table, friction exerted by the table acts opposite to the book's sliding motion. The book gradually slows because this friction produces a net force opposing its velocity.

Friction arises partly from microscopic irregularities and interactions between contacting surfaces. Its magnitude depends on the nature of the surfaces and how strongly they press against each other.

Static, sliding and rolling friction

Static friction acts between surfaces that are not sliding relative to one another. It prevents slipping and can adjust its magnitude to balance an applied force up to a maximum value.

For example, if a horizontal push of 3 N is applied to a box and the box remains at rest, static friction can act with a magnitude of 3 N in the opposite direction. The net horizontal force is then zero.

Sliding friction acts when 1 surface slides over another. It usually makes an already moving box easier to keep sliding than it was to start moving.

Rolling friction or rolling resistance is associated with a body rolling over a surface. In familiar school-level comparisons, rolling resistance is generally smaller than sliding friction for comparable conditions. This is why wheels and rollers make it easier to move many loads.

TypeConditionExample
Static frictionNo relative slidingShoe gripping the road
Sliding frictionSurfaces slideBook sliding on a table
Rolling frictionBody rollsWheel moving over a road

The commonly taught comparison is that maximum static friction is usually greater than sliding friction, and rolling resistance is generally smaller than sliding friction under comparable conditions. However, actual static friction is not always the largest force: it can be zero or can adjust to a small applied force.

Why friction is useful

Friction is essential for many everyday activities:

  • Walking: Static friction between the shoe and ground helps prevent backward slipping and allows forward movement.
  • Vehicle movement: Friction between tyres and road is needed for acceleration, braking and turning.
  • Writing: Friction enables a pencil or chalk to leave a mark on a surface.
  • Gripping: Friction helps a person hold objects without dropping them.

Grooves on shoe soles and tyre treads can improve practical grip under suitable surface conditions. Friction is therefore not merely a force that stops motion; it also makes controlled motion possible.

Why friction can be undesirable

Friction can oppose useful movement and convert part of the energy of motion into heat. It can also cause wear, as seen in shoe soles and moving mechanical parts.

To reduce unwanted friction, lubricants such as oil and grease may be used between moving surfaces. Wheels, rollers and ball bearings can reduce resistance by replacing much of the sliding contact with rolling contact.

Friction in fluids

Air and water also oppose the movement of objects through them. This resistive force is called fluid friction or drag.

Drag depends on factors such as an object's speed relative to the fluid, its shape and the nature of the fluid. For example, a moving cyclist experiences air resistance, while a swimmer experiences resistance from water.

How friction connects with Newton's laws

The motion of a ball slowing on the ground is explained by an unbalanced frictional force. If no net external force acted on it, Newton's first law predicts that it would continue at constant velocity.

Newton's second law connects the net force with acceleration through \(F=ma\). Newton's third law explains why the ground exerts a forward frictional force on a foot that pushes it backwards. These forces act on different objects.

More generally, distance and displacement describe how far an object travels and how its position changes; speed and velocity describe its rate of motion; and acceleration describes a change in velocity. The slope of a distance–time graph gives speed, while the slope of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration and its signed area gives displacement. Momentum is \(p=mv\), and the total momentum of a system is conserved when its net external force is zero.

Prelims focus

  • Friction opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide between contacting surfaces.
  • Static friction acts without relative sliding and can adjust up to a maximum.
  • Sliding friction acts during sliding; rolling resistance is generally smaller under comparable conditions.
  • Friction helps walking, gripping, braking and writing.
  • Lubricants and rollers reduce unwanted friction.
  • Drag is the resistive force associated with motion through a fluid.
  • Trap: Friction need not act opposite to the motion of an entire object; during walking, static friction from the ground can act forwards on the foot.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 12, 'Friction', sections 12.1–12.6, pp. 146–154, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, 'Force and Laws of Motion', sections 9.1–9.6, pp. 114–127, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', sections 8.1–8.6, pp. 98–112, 2018–19 print; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 'Friction', sections 9.1–9.6, consulted 2 November 2026.]
